Try Materials.Ai David Willson 06.24.2026 Manufacturing Insights Time to read: 11 min As product design cycles accelerate, the demand for large-format industrial 3D printing has shifted from rapid prototyping to functional applications. Moving beyond the constraints of consumer-grade desktop systems, large-scale 3D printing enables engineers to produce full-scale components, enclosures, jigs, and fixtures without the lead times associated with traditional tooling. What Is Large Format 3D Printing? In an industrial context, “large” format 3D printing refers to build volumes exceeding 500 mm in any dimension. While most consumer machines focus on smaller parts, large-scale 3D printing requires advanced thermal management, high-flow extrusion, or vat-based systems capable of maintaining structural integrity across larger volumes of material. Industrial 3D printing systems often accommodate parts up to 914 x 610 x 914 mm (36 x 24 x 36 in). There are two primary categories in 3D printing : consumer (“desktop scale”) and industrial additive manufacturing. Desktop-scale systems are normally entry-level solutions found in shared workspace and R&D labs. While cost-effective, many of them are limited by thermally uninsulated environments, filament flow rate constraints, and structural instability. Industrial large-format 3D printing moves the process out of the laboratory and into the production facility. These systems handle the unique processing demands of oversized printed parts with active thermal management of the print area, advanced filament extrusion dynamics, and the ability to process reinforced, high-temperature engineering thermoplastics. When designers begin laying out large 3D-printed parts, they have to consider more than just the shape of the final product. They have to think about the thermodynamic processes that will occur during the actual build. Transitioning to industrial-grade large-format printing aligns the machine’s engineering envelope with the geometry’s physics, ensuring the finished part is fully functional. 3D Printing Techniques for Large-Scale Parts By selecting the correct process, you can achieve consistent results in large-scale additive manufacturing: Large-Format FDM (Fused Deposition Modeling) Large-Format FDM is effective for fabricating lightweight manufacturing tooling, jigs/fixtures, and even massive functional parts like robotic end-effectors and structural housings. By scaling up to wide-diameter nozzles (typically 0.6 mm to 1.2 mm or larger) and high-diameter filament inputs, industrial FDM systems can process high-performance, carbon fiber-reinforced composites to deliver heavy-duty structural components. However, scaling a filament-fed FDM system up introduces a major thermodynamic bottleneck: the volumetric extrusion limit. The maximum print speed is fundamentally governed by how quickly heat can penetrate the core of a solid polymer wire as it passes through the hotend. To maintain structural integrity across a 500 mm+ build without stalling the drive gears, industrial large-format FDM printers utilize extended melt-zone hotends, dual-element heating arrays, and forced-convection active build chambers. These active thermal environments are critical for managing the inter-laminar bond strength of the part. If the ambient chamber temperature drops too far below the material’s glass transition temperature, the previously deposited bead will cool and solidify completely before the next layer arrives. This prevents the polymer chains from cross-linking and diffusing across the layer interface, resulting in brittle parts prone to splitting under load. For large-scale high-performance thermoplastic builds, maintaining tight control over this localized thermal gradient is the only way to prevent warping and ensure true structural performance. Large SLA (Stereolithography) Large SLA printing is the best option for oversized components where premium surface finishes and feature resolutions take priority. Using precise UV laser systems to cure liquid photopolymer resins, large SLA produces aesthetic prototypes, clear fluidic housings, and master patterns for low-volume urethane casting without visible layer lines. However, scaling a vat-based photopolymerization build-up introduces hydrodynamic and mechanical challenges that don’t exist on smaller platforms. Every time a new layer is cured, the build platform lifts vertically to break the vacuum seal between the freshly cured resin and the vat’s bottom membrane. For large-surface-area parts, these peel forces scale nonlinearly. If your geometry doesn’t feature robust support anchoring and deliberate cross-sectional optimization, these separation forces can tear the part completely off its scaffolding or warp fine features. Engineers must also account for low green strength. When an SLA part is inside the liquid resin vat, it exists in a partially cured, gel-like state before its final run in a UV post-curing oven. Oversized, heavy, or long overhanging features are highly susceptible to sagging, bowing, or shifting under their own weight during construction. To mitigate this green-state deflection, large SLA parts require specialized, high-density support webbing and localized wall variations designed specifically to resist gravity and peel-line dynamics. Pellet Extrusion (BAAM) When production timelines demand large volumetric deposition rates, industrial pellet extrusion—often referred to as Big Area Additive Manufacturing (BAAM)—is the most practical option. By melting raw plastic pellets directly in a high-output, screw-driven extruder mounted on a robotic arm or large gantry, these systems bypass the volumetric flow-rate limits of traditional filaments. However, this high speed comes at the expense of surface quality. Pellet systems use wide extrusion nozzles that deposit heavy plastic beads, typically 4 to 8 mm wide. This creates a very pronounced “stair-stepping” texture along the part walls. While it is an excellent, cost-effective solution for large structural foundations, foundry patterns, and heavy marine tooling, any tight-tolerance mating faces or cosmetic surfaces will require secondary CNC post-machining to achieve a functional finish. How Does Part Size Impact the Additive Manufacturing Process? Engineers must account for the following variables when 3D printing larger parts: Thermal Warp Controlling thermal warp in large-format prints requires managing the distinct cooling behaviors of different polymer structures. Amorphous thermoplastics, such as ABS or Polycarbonate , experience a gradual, linear contraction as they cool past their glass transition temperature. Because the outer shells of a large part cool faster than the insulated core, residual internal tensile stresses accumulate, leading to severe dimensional warping or bed separation. Semi-crystalline polymers like Nylon (PA12) present an even greater challenge. They undergo a sudden, sharp volumetric drop during the crystallization phase of cooling. Without an actively managed, heated build environment to slow this crystallization down, large-format parts will warp or crack along the layer lines before the print job finishes. Internal Stress Concentration The mismatch in cooling rates between the outer surface and the interior of a bulky part can create stresses that lead to internal voids or layer delamination. Proper design should remove excess bulk, and print parameters should be precisely tuned to minimize internal stresses. Mechanical Anisotropy Because all additive manufacturing processes are inherently layer-based, parts are naturally anisotropic. In standard industrial FDM profiles, you can expect about a 20% to 45% reduction in tensile strength and inter-laminar fracture toughness along the vertical Z-axis compared to the continuous X-Y plane. This performance drop happens because the polymer chains cannot fully diffuse and entangle across the layer interfaces before the previously deposited plastic cools. When engineering large, load-bearing fixtures or enclosures, you shouldn’t rely on isotropic material datasheets without accounting for print orientation. CAD models should be oriented so that primary structural stress vectors run parallel to the build plate, utilizing the continuous strength of the extruded material strands rather than relying on the weaker layer joints. Build Time Scaling In additive manufacturing, build time doesn’t always scale linearly with part volume. It scales with the cross-sectional area of each layer and the layer count, both of which depend on the Z-height. For example, doubling a part’s Z-height doubles the layer count and proportionally increases total build time, independent of volume. Part Post-Processing Large-format parts require proportionally greater effort for support removal, surface finishing, and cleaning. The increased surface area and complex internal geometries common in large prints significantly extend post-processing time. Large-Format 3D Printing Compared to Traditional Large-Scale Tooling For large-scale components, the choice between additive manufacturing and traditional tooling comes down to trade-offs between speed, volume, and cost. Additive manufacturing (3D printing) is an agile solution that allows rapid iteration of innovative new designs, while traditional methods such as injection molding and machining remain the standard in high-volume manufacturing of mechanically strong parts. Large-Format 3D Printing vs. Molding/Machining Technical Factor Large-Format 3D Printing Large Injection Molding / Machining Upfront Tooling Cost $0 (direct from CAD) Very high (large molds/fixtures) Geometric Freedom High (internal channels & lightened lattices) Constrained by tool reach or draft angles Lead Time 1 to 5 days Weeks to months (for tooling fabrication) Mechanical Isotropy Anisotropic (depends on print orientation, material, and process) Excellent (mostly uniform grain or material density) Production Volume Ideal for 1–50 parts (prototypes/fixtures) Ideal for 500+ parts (mass production) Dimensional Tolerancing Range ±0.2 mm to ±0.5 mm (Highly dependent on process, thermal management, and material) ±0.02 mm to ±0.1 mm (Governed by rigid machine geometry and tool setups) DFM Strategies for Large-Scale 3D-Printed Parts The inherent thermal and structural challenges of oversized parts demand a deliberate design approach. The following Design for Manufacturing (DFM) strategies are essential for producing large-scale 3D-printed parts that maintain dimensional accuracy and mechanical integrity. Managing Infill, Wall Topography, and Mass Reduction Avoiding 100% infill is recommended. Using gyroid or honeycomb infill reduces part mass and thermal inertia, which significantly decreases the risk of warping while maintaining the rigidity of the print. Optimizing infill patterns and maximizing the amount of contact area between the build plate and the object being printed (for bed adhesion) helps counter the effects of thermal expansion and increase stiffness. Selecting a material like carbon fiber-filled nylon can also help reduce thermal expansion relative to many standard printing materials. Structural Ribs for Large, Flat Surfaces Large, flat surfaces are prone to bowing. Instead of increasing wall thickness uniformly, add ribs or gussets to the non-critical faces of the part (typically the interior or back side) to stiffen the geometry against thermal warping while leaving the critical face smooth and uninterrupted. Splitting Large Models: Joints and Sectioning When a design exceeds a machine’s build volume, the CAD model must be subdivided into sections. A basic dovetail or puzzle joint may be sufficient for visual models, but functional jigs and enclosures require split lines treated as engineered interfaces: Design a Bond-Line Gap : Incorporate a uniform clearance of 0.1–0.2 mm between mating surfaces to allow for part tolerances and to provide space for structural epoxy or polyurethane adhesive to seat properly. Use a Hybrid Joining Strategy : Don’t rely on adhesive alone. Combine interlocking keys or dovetails with hidden mechanical fasteners—press-fit alignment pins for shear loads, and pocket screws or heat-set threaded inserts for tensile loads. Export as Multi-Body STEP Files : Export directly from your native CAD software as a multi-body STEP file to preserve geometric alignment and coordinate registration across all joint interfaces before sending files to print. Axis Orientation Strategies for Strength If a part requires a tall Z-height, orient primary stress zones to run parallel to the build plate (X-Y plane) to leverage the higher isotropic strength of the extrusion lines. This exploits the near-isotropic strength of the fused filament direction rather than relying on the weaker interlayer bonds along the Z-axis. Choosing the right material is as critical as choosing the right process. Fictiv’s Ultimate Guide to 3D Printing Materials and Applications covers material properties, process compatibility, and application-specific recommendations in detail. Secondary Processing: Joining and Finishing Large Parts When a planned product is too big to build with one print, the components must be assembled using mechanical fasteners , solvent bonding, or adhesives . A manufacturing partner that specializes in the assembly and precision finishing required to blend jointed seams can help ensure the finished part acts as a single, cohesive unit. Streamlining Large-Part Additive Manufacturing Sourcing Manufacturing large 3D-printed parts at an industrial scale involves navigating complex design, sourcing, and processing plans. Poor decisions can result in problems ranging from build plate adhesion failures to long, unpredictable print cycles. Fictiv reduces these risks through automated DFM feedback that flags geometry, design, and process mismatch issues before your part hits the printer. With access to industrial-grade build volumes and expert multi-body assembly guidance, Fictiv is your partner in scaling from initial CAD model to shop floor production. Upload your CAD model today to start a free 3DP quote. FAQs About Large Format 3D Printing What is considered “large format” in 3D printing? In an industrial context, large format typically refers to build volumes exceeding 500 mm in any single dimension. Consumer desktop machines generally fall well below this threshold, while industrial systems can accommodate parts up to 914 x 610 x 914 mm (36 x 24 x 36 in) or larger, depending on the platform and process. Fictiv’s manufacturing network includes access to industrial-grade large-format systems capable of producing parts at this scale. Which large-format 3D printing process is best for my application? It depends on your part requirements. FDM is the most versatile choice for functional tooling, jigs, and fixtures where strength and durability matter. SLA is preferred when fine detail and smooth surface finish are critical, such as for high-fidelity prototypes. Pellet extrusion is best suited for very large structural parts where build speed and material volume take priority over surface quality. How do I prevent warping in large 3D printed parts? Warping is primarily driven by uneven thermal contraction during cooling. The most effective countermeasures include using optimized infill patterns such as gyroid or honeycomb to reduce thermal mass, maximizing the bed-adhesion contact area, selecting low-shrinkage materials like carbon fiber-filled nylon, and incorporating structural ribs into large flat surfaces to resist bowing. What should I do if my part is too large for the printer’s build volume? The part will need to be sectioned in CAD and printed as multiple pieces. Design keyed joints or dovetail features at the split interfaces to ensure self-alignment and maximize bonding surface area. Export the assembly as a multi-body STP file for geometry registration, then export each section as a separate STL for printing. Sections can then be joined using mechanical fasteners, adhesives, or solvent bonding. Fictiv’s manufacturing partners specialize in precision finishing and assembly of multi-body large-format parts. How does large-format 3D printing compare to traditional machining or injection molding for large parts? For low volumes and iterative design, large-format 3D printing offers significant advantages: no upfront tooling cost, lead times of one to five days, and geometric freedom that traditional processes can’t match. However, for high-volume production of 500 or more parts, injection molding and machining remain superior due to better mechanical isotropy, tighter tolerances, and lower per-part cost at scale. Fictiv supports both additive and traditional manufacturing, making it straightforward to transition from prototype to production without switching suppliers.

It scales with the cross-sectional area of each layer and the layer count, both of which depend on the Z-height. For example, doubling a part’s Z-height doubles the layer count and proportionally increases total build time, independent of volume. Part Post-Processing Large-format parts require proportionally greater effort for support removal, surface finishing, and cleaning. The increased surface area and complex internal geometries common in large prints significantly extend post-processing time. Large-Format 3D Printing Compared to Traditional Large-Scale Tooling For large-scale components, the choice between additive manufacturing and traditional tooling comes down to trade-offs between speed, volume, and cost. Additive manufacturing (3D printing) is an agile solution that allows rapid iteration of innovative new designs, while traditional methods such as injection molding and machining remain the standard in high-volume manufacturing of mechanically strong parts. Large-Format 3D Printing vs. Molding/Machining Technical Factor Large-Format 3D Printing Large Injection Molding / Machining Upfront Tooling Cost $0 (direct from CAD) Very high (large molds/fixtures) Geometric Freedom High (internal channels & lightened lattices) Constrained by tool reach or draft angles Lead Time 1 to 5 days Weeks to months (for tooling fabrication) Mechanical Isotropy Anisotropic (depends on print orientation, material, and process) Excellent (mostly uniform grain or material density) Production Volume Ideal for 1–50 parts (prototypes/fixtures) Ideal for 500+ parts (mass production) Dimensional Tolerancing Range ±0.2 mm to ±0.5 mm (Highly dependent on process, thermal management, and material) ±0.02 mm to ±0.1 mm (Governed by rigid machine geometry and tool setups) DFM Strategies for Large-Scale 3D-Printed Parts The inherent thermal and structural challenges of oversized parts demand a deliberate design approach. The following Design for Manufacturing (DFM) strategies are essential for producing large-scale 3D-printed parts that maintain dimensional accuracy and mechanical integrity. Managing Infill, Wall Topography, and Mass Reduction Avoiding 100% infill is recommended. Using gyroid or honeycomb infill reduces part mass and thermal inertia, which significantly decreases the risk of warping while maintaining the rigidity of the print. Optimizing infill patterns and maximizing the amount of contact area between the build plate and the object being printed (for bed adhesion) helps counter the effects of thermal expansion and increase stiffness. Selecting a material like carbon fiber-filled nylon can also help reduce thermal expansion relative to many standard printing materials. Structural Ribs for Large, Flat Surfaces Large, flat surfaces are prone to bowing. Instead of increasing wall thickness uniformly, add ribs or gussets to the non-critical faces of the part (typically the interior or back side) to stiffen the geometry against thermal warping while leaving the critical face smooth and uninterrupted. Splitting Large Models: Joints and Sectioning When a design exceeds a machine’s build volume, the CAD model must be subdivided into sections. A basic dovetail or puzzle joint may be sufficient for visual models, but functional jigs and enclosures require split lines treated as engineered interfaces: Design a Bond-Line Gap : Incorporate a uniform clearance of 0.1–0.2 mm between mating surfaces to allow for part tolerances and to provide space for structural epoxy or polyurethane adhesive to seat properly. Use a Hybrid Joining Strategy : Don’t rely on adhesive alone. Combine interlocking keys or dovetails with hidden mechanical fasteners—press-fit alignment pins for shear loads, and pocket screws or heat-set threaded inserts for tensile loads. Export as Multi-Body STEP Files : Export directly from your native CAD software as a multi-body STEP file to preserve geometric alignment and coordinate registration across all joint interfaces before sending files to print. Axis Orientation Strategies for Strength If a part requires a tall Z-height, orient primary stress zones to run parallel to the build plate (X-Y plane) to leverage the higher isotropic strength of the extrusion lines. This exploits the near-isotropic strength of the fused filament direction rather than relying on the weaker interlayer bonds along the Z-axis. Choosing the right material is as critical as choosing the right process. Fictiv’s Ultimate Guide to 3D Printing Materials and Applications covers material properties, process compatibility, and application-specific recommendations in detail. Secondary Processing: Joining and Finishing Large Parts When a planned product is too big to build with one print, the components must be assembled using mechanical fasteners , solvent bonding, or adhesives . A manufacturing partner that specializes in the assembly and precision finishing required to blend jointed seams can help ensure the finished part acts as a single, cohesive unit. Streamlining Large-Part Additive Manufacturing Sourcing Manufacturing large 3D-printed parts at an industrial scale involves navigating complex design, sourcing, and processing plans. Poor decisions can result in problems ranging from build plate adhesion failures to long, unpredictable print cycles. Fictiv reduces these risks through automated DFM feedback that flags geometry, design, and process mismatch issues before your part hits the printer. With access to industrial-grade build volumes and expert multi-body assembly guidance, Fictiv is your partner in scaling from initial CAD model to shop floor production. Upload your CAD model today to start a free 3DP quote. FAQs About Large Format 3D Printing What is considered “large format” in 3D printing? In an industrial context, large format typically refers to build volumes exceeding 500 mm in any single dimension. Consumer desktop machines generally fall well below this threshold, while industrial systems can accommodate parts up to 914 x 610 x 914 mm (36 x 24 x 36 in) or larger, depending on the platform and process. Fictiv’s manufacturing network includes access to industrial-grade large-format systems capable of producing parts at this scale. Which large-format 3D printing process is best for my application? It depends on your part requirements. FDM is the most versatile choice for functional tooling, jigs, and fixtures where strength and durability matter. SLA is preferred when fine detail and smooth surface finish are critical, such as for high-fidelity prototypes. Pellet extrusion is best suited for very large structural parts where build speed and material volume take priority over surface quality. How do I prevent warping in large 3D printed parts? Warping is primarily driven by uneven thermal contraction during cooling. The most effective countermeasures include using optimized infill patterns such as gyroid or honeycomb to reduce thermal mass, maximizing the bed-adhesion contact area, selecting low-shrinkage materials like carbon fiber-filled nylon, and incorporating structural ribs into large flat surfaces to resist bowing. What should I do if my part is too large for the printer’s build volume? The part will need to be sectioned in CAD and printed as multiple pieces. Design keyed joints or dovetail features at the split interfaces to ensure self-alignment and maximize bonding surface area. Export the assembly as a multi-body STP file for geometry registration, then export each section as a separate STL for printing. Sections can then be joined using mechanical fasteners, adhesives, or solvent bonding. Fictiv’s manufacturing partners specialize in precision finishing and assembly of multi-body large-format parts. How does large-format 3D printing compare to traditional machining or injection molding for large parts? For low volumes and iterative design, large-format 3D printing offers significant advantages: no upfront tooling cost, lead times of one to five days, and geometric freedom that traditional processes can’t match. However, for high-volume production of 500 or more parts, injection molding and machining remain superior due to better mechanical isotropy, tighter tolerances, and lower per-part cost at scale. Fictiv supports both additive and traditional manufacturing, making it straightforward to transition from prototype to production without switching suppliers.

Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Considerations for Single-Point and Multi-Point Grounding PCB Layout Considerations for Single-Point and Multi-Point Grounding by: Mila Oct 27,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Layout PCB Grounding Techniques PCB Grounding Guidelines PCB grounding is an important part of PCB layout , affecting circuit stability, noise levels, signal integrity, and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC). Different circuits have different grounding requirements, and single-point grounding, multi-point grounding, and mixed grounding each have their own applications. This article explains the differences between these grounding techniques and highlights key considerations for effective PCB grounding. 1. Basic Principles of PCB Grounding In a PCB, ground provides a voltage reference for the circuit and a return path for current. Ideally, the ground plane should have low impedance. However, copper traces, vias, and connection structures introduce parasitic resistance and inductance. As frequency increases, parasitic inductance generally has a greater impact on grounding impedance. Therefore, PCB grounding design should consider not only DC resistance but also signal frequency, return paths, and reference-plane continuity. Key considerations include: Minimize grounding impedance: Use ground planes, copper pours, and vias appropriately to reduce unnecessary impedance along grounding paths. Control noise coupling: Arrange sensitive analog circuits, digital circuits, and power circuits to minimize interference. Maintain continuous return paths: For high-speed signals, avoid reference-plane splits and other structures that force return currents to take detours. Choose an appropriate grounding technique: No single grounding method is suitable for every PCB layout. 2. Three Common PCB Grounding Techniques （Single-Point vs. Multi-Point Grounding in PCB Design） Single-Point Grounding Single-point grounding connects multiple circuit grounds at a designated point to help reduce common-impedance coupling between circuit sections. This technique is often used in low-frequency analog circuits, sensor circuits, and other applications where coupling through shared ground paths is a concern. Key design considerations include: Choose the connection point carefully: Avoid routing large return currents through ground paths shared with sensitive analog circuits. Keep grounding paths short: Minimize unnecessary detours while maintaining appropriate electrical connections. Consider high-frequency behavior: Single-point grounding is not always suitable for high-frequency circuits, as long grounding wires can introduce additional inductance. Multi-Point Grounding Multi-point grounding connects a circuit ground to a ground plane or grounding structure at multiple locations. This approach can shorten grounding paths and reduce impedance at high frequencies. It is commonly used in high-speed digital circuits, RF circuits, and designs that require low-impedance high-frequency return paths. Key design considerations include: Prioritize ground-plane continuity: Provide a stable reference path for signals, especially high-speed signals. Place ground vias appropriately: Add vias near connectors, shielding structures, and other locations where they help shorten return paths. Avoid unnecessary return-path detours: Check whether ground-plane slots, splits, or poorly planned connections could interrupt return currents. More ground vias do not automatically result in better grounding. Their placement and the overall return-path structure are equally important. Mixed Grounding Mixed grounding combines different grounding strategies according to the requirements of individual circuit sections. For example, a low-frequency sensitive analog circuit may use a designated single-point connection, while a high-speed digital circuit relies on a continuous ground plane and multiple grounding connections. This approach is useful for mixed-signal PCBs and complex systems with different frequency and current requirements. Key design considerations include: Separate circuit functions through layout: Arrange analog and digital components appropriately and route signals to reduce noise coupling. Evaluate ground separation carefully: Do not assume that all mixed-signal circuits require split ground planes. Plan return paths across circuit sections: If a split ground plane is necessary, ensure that signals crossing between sections have appropriate return paths. Comparison of PCB Grounding Techniques 3. PCB Grounding Guidelines for Single-Point and Multi-Point Grounding Single-Point Grounding Guidelines The main goal of single-point grounding is to control common impedance and prevent current from one circuit section from interfering with another through a shared grounding path. Plan ground connections carefully: Avoid routing large return currents through grounding paths shared with sensitive analog circuits. Minimize unnecessary path lengths: Reduce detours while maintaining appropriate circuit connections. Consider high-frequency performance: Do not select single-point grounding solely based on the number of circuit sections. Its suitability depends on the frequency range and circuit characteristics. Multi-Point Grounding Guidelines The main goal of multi-point grounding is to provide low-impedance, continuous return paths for current. Maintain ground-plane continuity: For high-speed signals, avoid routing across split reference-plane regions. Place ground vias strategically: Position vias near connectors, shielding structures, and other locations where they improve return-path continuity. The exact placement depends on the circuit and PCB structure. Minimize return-path detours: Check whether ground-plane slots, splits, or reference-layer changes could affect the return paths of critical signals. 4. Grounding Design for Mixed-Signal PCBs Mixed-signal PCBs contain both analog and digital circuits. Digital switching can generate transient currents, while analog circuits may be sensitive to small amounts of noise. The goal is to control noise coupling and provide appropriate return paths for different signals. Arrange Components into Functional Zones Arrange analog circuits, digital circuits, and switching power supplies according to their functions. Keep sensitive analog signal paths short and avoid routing high-speed digital signals through sensitive analog areas. For switching power supplies, pay particular attention to switching nodes and high-frequency current loops. Avoid placing these noisy areas close to sensitive analog circuits whenever possible. Handle AGND and DGND Carefully AGND and DGND refer to analog ground and digital ground, respectively. However, this does not mean that every PCB must separate them into two independent ground planes. For many mixed-signal circuits, a continuous ground plane combined with careful component placement, signal routing, and current-path management is a sensible starting point. If an IC datasheet specifies that AGND and DGND must be connected at a particular location, follow the manufacturer's recommendations. When using a 0-ohm resistor, ferrite bead, or another component to connect separate ground nets, evaluate its impedance and noise effects for the specific circuit rather than treating it as a universal solution. Maintain Continuous Signal Return Paths For high-speed signals, return current typically flows in the reference plane near the signal trace. If a trace crosses a ground-plane split, slot, or reference-layer transition, the return current may be forced to take a longer path. This can increase loop area and electromagnetic interference (EMI). Therefore, PCB layout should provide continuous reference planes for critical high-speed signals whenever possible. When a signal changes reference layers, verify that its return path remains adequately connected. （Mixed-Signal PCB Layout and Grounding Design） 5. Common PCB Grounding Mistakes and Solutions Conclusion There is no single grounding method that works for every PCB layout . Single-point grounding is suitable for some low-frequency sensitive circuits, multi-point grounding is often used where low-impedance high-frequency return paths are required, and mixed grounding combines strategies according to the needs of different circuit sections. In practical PCB layout, prioritize ground-plane continuity, current-loop design, common impedance, and signal return paths. Use IC datasheets, reference designs, and test results to guide design decisions. A well-planned grounding strategy can help reduce noise coupling, improve signal integrity, and enhance overall PCB stability. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Engineer 15x15 Adressible RGB LED Panel [PCB Assembly] This project is a custom 15 × 15 RGB LED panel designed as the display core of a pixel-art mood lamp. Its 170 × 170 mm PCB contains 225 individually addressable Worldsemi WS2812B-2427-V6 LEDs at 10 mm spacing. A serpentine data chain allows an external microcontroller to control the entire panel through one signal output. The board uses a three-wire DATA, GND and regulated 5 V interface, with supply capacitors, an input pulldown and an output test pad for troubleshooting. Intended applications include pixel art, animated patterns, ambient lighting and a clock Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.

Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Engineer 15x15 Adressible RGB LED Panel [PCB Assembly] This project is a custom 15 × 15 RGB LED panel designed as the display core of a pixel-art mood lamp. Its 170 × 170 mm PCB contains 225 individually addressable Worldsemi WS2812B-2427-V6 LEDs at 10 mm spacing. A serpentine data chain allows an external microcontroller to control the entire panel through one signal output. The board uses a three-wire DATA, GND and regulated 5 V interface, with supply capacitors, an input pulldown and an output test pad for troubleshooting. Intended applications include pixel art, animated patterns, ambient lighting and a clock Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Begallie 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. Each PCB has a unique function for a particular product. Therefore, producing a PCB is a complex process of many steps. This overview covers the most important steps when producing a multilayer PCB. When you order PCBs from the PCBWay, you are buying quality that pays for itself over time. This is guaranteed through a product specification and quality control that is far more stringent than other suppliers, and ensures that the product delivers what it promises. In the production flow below you can see where the PCBWay process is unique or goes beyond the IPC standard. Making a PCB - PCB Manufacture step by step Click the icon to view the details 01.Pre Production Engineering 02.Board Cutting 03.Print inner layers 04.Etch inner layers 05.AOI 06.Lay-up and bond 07.Drilling the PCB 08.Electroless copper deposition 09.Image the outer layers 10.Plating 11.Etch outer layer 12.AOI 13.Soldermask 14.Surface finish 15.Profile 16.Electrical test 17.Final inspection 18.Packaging 19.Delivery 20.After-Sales Service 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. Hide Details 01-1.Preparing the phototools Artwork Master is PCB production in the key steps, which directly affect the quality of the final product quality,An accurately scaled configuration of electronic data used to produce the artwork master or production master. Artwork Master – The photographic image of the PCB pattern on film used to produce the circuit board, usually on a 1:1 scale.In general, there are three types of Artwork Master:(1) Conductive Pattern (2) solder mask (3) Silkscreen Put away 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. Hide Details 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. Hide Details 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. Hide Details 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. Hide Details 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. Hide Details 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill Hide Details 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. Hide Details 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Hide Details 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. Hide Details 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. Hide Details 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. Hide Details 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Hide Details 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. Hide Details 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. Hide Details 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. Hide Details 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. Hide Details 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport.
